catalog_quote: The vowel ɛ The vowel ɛ is a mid front unrounded vowel [e̞]. In normal speech, this vowel often laxes when adjacent to a velar consonant, being realized as the mid central vowel [ə]. Sometimes, this laxing also occurs when the vowel is utterance final. The laxing is less likely to occur if the vowel is in a position associated with stress (as indicated by an apparent increase in intensity), such as root initial, and is often “corrected” in careful speech. Note that stress as a feature of the sound system has not been studied beyond the observances made here. ... [Ch.4, p.57:] Nchane is a tonal language with a tonal system comprising three level tones and several contour tones. This distinguishes it from the two-tone systems commonly associated with Narrow Bantu languages, although many Bantoid languages of the area also report more than two level tones ... tone_statements.quote: Seven phonetic tone melodies have been identified in Mungong: three level tones (H, M and L) and four contour tones (HM, ML, MH, LM). [...] At this point in time, many minimal tone pairs have been found for words that contrast high tone, mid tone, low tone and falling tones. However, examples of minimal tone pairs involving rising tones are very rare. [...] [§3.3] Tone in Mungong is contrastive and most tone performs a lexical function by differentiating between two or more words that differ in pronunciation only by pitch.

tone_statements.quote: The Nchane tone system shows seven distinct tone melodies which are made up of three level tones: L, M and H. Each of these level tones is observed as a simple tone melody. The three tones also combine to make four different contour tone melodies: three falling melodies (HM, HL and ML) and one rising melody (MH). ... Automatic downstep of H tones happens when preceded by a non-H tone, resulting in a lowering of the tone register.
tone_statements.locator: p. 2, sec. 1.3 The Nchane Tone System
tone_statements.summary: 3 levels, 7 root melodies (contours = sequences); downstep described is automatic (HLH/HMH); floating (H)(L)(M) used; super-low derived. forms_shown a floor.

tone_statements.citation: Boutwell, Richard L. 2011. Mungong Phonology Sketch. Yaoundé: SIL. iv+26 pp. Manuscript, SIL Cameroon Language & Culture Archives entry 43195. (Cited in Boutwell 2020: 378 with 'https://www.silcam.org/resources/archives/43195' and in the 2022 Mungong Orthography Guide p.29.)
tone_statements.quote: Mungong has three contrastive level tones: High (H), Mid (M) and Low (L). It also utilizes contour tone in various falling and rising patterns. The degree to which the contour tones are truly contrastive, and therefore phonologically significant, needs further analysis. ... Tone in Mungong serves to distinguish a number of nouns and verbs (lexical tone) and to mark the plural form of gender 9/10 nouns (grammatical tone). Every syllable bears tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 16, sections 4.1 Level and Contour Tones and 4.3 Functionality of Tone
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones H, M, L; contours HM, ML, MH, LM listed (Table 5) but contrastive status left open ('combinations of these level tones', p.25). Minimal sets ex.14-16; describes the Mungong variety.

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal, no stress rule stated' rests on the 2020 Leiden reference grammar, held with text; both deciding passages are verbatim at the stated pages (p.39/PDF 63 and p.57/PDF 81). The grammar itself says stress has not been studied beyond an impressionistic root-initial intensity remark, which the record's the primary-stress rule already captures. The two earlier SIL sketches by the same author (downloaded now from the Internet Archive, are silent on stress and describe the same three-level tone system. The only unheld substantial work, Richards 1991, is an unpublished Paris thesis that Boutwell reports as a tone analysis; no instrumental or prosodic study of Nchane was found. Nothing suggests a reclassify.

sources.note: Ch.3 'Tone' (pp.12-21): seven phonetic tone melodies - three level tones H, M, L and four contours HM, ML (falling), MH, LM (rising); many minimal pairs for H/M/L/falling, rising-tone minimal pairs very rare; tone is lexically contrastive; grammatical tone: gender 9/10 plural marked by H, hortative, general future vs immediate past, functor mwo/mwó, relative pronouns vs associative markers; orthography follows the Nooni model (diacritics disambiguate grammar/lexicon rather than writing surface tone).
